raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan introduced angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) as a disease-modifying strategy in heart failure. The drug couples valsartan-mediated blockade of angiotensin II type 1 receptors with sacubitril-mediated neprilysin inhibition, thereby augmenting endogenous natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and related vasoactive substrates while suppressing maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone signaling. Early phase data in HFpEF showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and left atrial reverse remodeling than valsartan, supporting proof of concept before outcomes trials [1]. Mechanistically, ARNI therapy appears to improve loading conditions, natriuresis, vascular function, and myocardial remodeling, although not every proposed pathway has translated into measurable clinical benefit [25,29].

The pivotal evidence is in chronic HFrEF. In PARADIGM-HF, 8399 ambulatory patients with symptomatic HFrEF tolerated run-in therapy and were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril; sacubitril/valsartan reduced cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, first heart-failure hospitalization, and all-cause death [2]. Subsequent analyses suggested benefit across clinical-risk strata, including patients with recent decompensation, across systolic blood pressure categories, and when recurrent—not only first—heart-failure hospitalizations were counted [3,4,6]. Patient-centered outcomes also favored ARNI: health status and physical/social limitations deteriorated less with sacubitril/valsartan than with enalapril [5]. Safety signals were consistent with vasodilatory therapy: symptomatic hypotension was more frequent, whereas cough, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment were generally less frequent than with enalapril; in patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, severe hyperkalemia was reduced [8]. Ancillary analyses also reported lower loop-diuretic requirements and modest improvements in glycemic control among patients with diabetes [7,9].

Evidence now supports initiation during or soon after hospitalization for worsening HFrEF. PIONEER-HF randomized stabilized inpatients with acute decompensated HFrEF and showed larger NT-proBNP reductions with sacubitril/valsartan than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [10]. Benefits were directionally consistent even among patients achieving lower doses [13]. TRANSITION showed that pre-discharge and early post-discharge initiation were both feasible after hemodynamic stabilization, while TITRATION demonstrated that slower up-titration improved tolerability in patients with lower prior renin–angiotensin system blocker exposure [11,12]. Reverse-remodeling data strengthened biological plausibility: PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reductions after ARNI initiation to improvements in left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction, whereas EVALUATE-HF did not show improvement in central aortic stiffness, implying that reverse remodeling is not explained solely by large-artery effects [14,15]. In advanced HFrEF, however, tolerability is more problematic: LIFE run-in data showed frequent intolerance even to low-dose sacubitril/valsartan, underscoring the need for blood pressure, renal, and congestion assessment before initiation [16,17].

In HFpEF and HFmrEF, the evidence is more nuanced. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested fewer heart-failure hospitalizations, with signals of greater benefit in women and in patients with ejection fraction below the normal range [18,19]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF found that benefit varied continuously by ejection fraction and appeared to extend into HFmrEF, particularly for heart-failure hospitalization [20]. PARAGON-HF also demonstrated blood-pressure lowering in patients with apparent resistant hypertension, an important practical effect in HFpEF [21]. PARALLAX reduced NT-proBNP but did not improve 6-minute walk distance, illustrating discordance between biomarkers and functional endpoints [22]. PARAGLIDE-HF, enrolling patients with EF >40% after worsening heart failure, reduced NT-proBNP more than valsartan; pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF analyses suggested reduced worsening heart-failure events, especially when EF was below normal, but with more symptomatic hypotension [23,24].

Current guidelines therefore place sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for HFrEF, preferably replacing ACE inhibitors or ARBs when tolerated, with a 36-hour ACE-inhibitor washout to reduce angioedema risk [26-28]. In HFmrEF and selected HFpEF—particularly EF at the lower end of the “preserved” range, women, hypertensive patients, or those with recent worsening heart failure—ARNI is a reasonable individualized option rather than a universal mandate. Practical use requires starting dose selection based on blood pressure, renal function, potassium, prior ACE inhibitor/ARB exposure, and frailty, followed by deliberate titration and monitoring. Observational hemodynamic-monitoring data and trial substudies support potential diuretic-sparing effects, but congestion management remains essential [30]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan has transformed HFrEF care and occupies an evidence-supported but more selective role across the mildly reduced and preserved ejection-fraction spectrum.
